bases.name: Stock
bases.notes: Chicken or veg cube. Use chicken for meat dishes, veg for fish or vegetarian.

bases.name: Light coconut milk
bases.sw_note: ~2.5 syns per 100ml light — one tin split 5 ways is manageable

aromatics.name: Onion + garlic
aromatics.notes: Base of every sauce. Always start here.

aromatics.name: Ginger
aromatics.notes: Add for Asian and Indian. Keeps 3 weeks in the fridge.

aromatics.name: Lemongrass paste
aromatics.notes: Tube — keeps forever. Thai and Vietnamese.

spice_profiles.name: Indian
spice_profiles.spices: 1 tsp cumin + 1 tsp ground coriander + 0.5 tsp turmeric + 1 tsp garam masala

spice_profiles.name: North African / Middle Eastern
spice_profiles.spices: 1 tsp cumin + 1 tsp ground coriander + 0.5 tsp cinnamon + 1 tsp paprika

depth.name: Tomato paste
depth.notes: Adds body and richness. Use in all tomato-based sauces.

depth.name: Worcestershire sauce
depth.notes: Good in any tomato-based sauce and in the French-style.

depth.name: Soy sauce
depth.notes: Asian sauces. Light soy for delicate dishes, dark for richer ones.

depth.name: Fish sauce
depth.notes: Very strong. Easy to overdo. Thai and Vietnamese. Can also sneak 1 tsp into Italian for depth.

depth.name: White miso
depth.sw_note: Check brand — typically 1-2 syns per tbsp. Keeps months in the fridge.
depth.notes: Japanese, Chinese, Korean. Also works as a general umami booster in stocks.

depth.name: Peanut butter
depth.sw_note: ~3 syns per tbsp — 2 tbsp split 5 ways is about 1.2 syns each
depth.notes: West African and Thai. Use smooth. Thickens the sauce naturally.

fresh_herbs.name: Coriander
fresh_herbs.use: Stir in at end or scatter as garnish. Never cook it.

fresh_herbs.name: Italian herbs
fresh_herbs.use: Fresh basil stirred in at end. Dried oregano or dried basil can go in earlier.

fresh_herbs.name: Flat-leaf parsley
fresh_herbs.use: Stirred in at end or garnish.

thickener.name: Thickening granules
thickener.notes: Add at end to any stock-based sauce — stir in gradually until you reach the consistency you want. Not needed for tomato-based sauces which reduce naturally in the oven. Check SW syn value on your brand but typically negligible per portion.

dressing_extras.name: Capers
dressing_extras.notes: Jar — keeps for months. Briny and punchy. Use straight from the jar, no prep.

dressing_extras.name: Dijon mustard
dressing_extras.notes: Emulsifies dressings so they don't split. Adds mild heat without affecting kids.

dressing_extras.name: Balsamic vinegar
dressing_extras.sw_note: ~1 syn per tbsp — check brand. Use sparingly.
dressing_extras.notes: Richer and sweeter than red wine vinegar. Good in warmer salads and roasted veg dressings.

dressing_extras.name: Tahini
dressing_extras.sw_note: ~3 syns per tbsp — worth it split across 5
dressing_extras.notes: Sesame paste. Thickens dressings, adds nuttiness. Middle Eastern and Mediterranean.

ingredients: 1 large onion or 3 shallots, finely diced
recipe_5.method: Soften shallots and garlic gently — don't let them colour. Add stock and Worcestershire. Simmer and reduce by about a third. Thicken with granules to your liking. Add lemon and parsley off the heat. Clean and simple — the protein should be the main event here.

elevate.tip: A small glass to deglaze after softening the shallots — reduce by half before adding the stock for complexity and acidity.
Use instead of flat-leaf parsley for a more distinctly French result. The aniseed note is a classic pairing with chicken and fish.

ingredients: handful fresh basil or 1 tsp dried oregano
recipe_5.method: Soften onion and garlic in cast iron. Add tomatoes, paste, Worcestershire, vinegar, salt, pepper. Into 180°C oven for 25-30 mins until reduced and slightly caramelised at the edges. Stir in herbs just before serving.

elevate.tip: Half a teaspoon stirred in at the start — dissolves completely and adds umami depth without any fishy flavour.
Drop a piece in while it oven-braises and remove before serving. Adds a savouriness that's hard to put your finger on.

recipe_5.method: Soften onion and garlic. Add spices and stir for 1 min before adding everything else. 180°C oven 25-30 mins. Smokier and earthier than Italian — works particularly well with fish.

elevate.tip: A small glass to deglaze after the aromatics — the alcohol cooks off, leaving a subtle nutty sweetness that's very Spanish.
A pinch bloomed in a tablespoon of hot water, stirred in with the tomatoes. Changes the whole personality of the sauce.

sauces.name: Salsa Roja
sauces.adult_heat_note: Chili flakes or fresh chili at the table

recipe_5.method: Soften onion and garlic. Toast spices 1 min. Add tomatoes and lime. 180°C oven 25 mins. Stir in coriander at the end. Chili on the table.

elevate.tip: A tablespoon gives smoky, complex heat that goes far beyond chilli flakes — stir in with the tomatoes.
A square of 85% stirred in at the very end. Classic Mexican mole trick — adds depth without tasting chocolatey.

ingredients: handful fresh coriander or flat-leaf parsley
recipe_5.method: Soften aromatics, toast spices 1 min. Add tomatoes and paste. 180°C oven 25-30 mins. The cinnamon is what makes this — don't skip it. Stir in herbs at end.

elevate.tip: A quarter, rind only, finely sliced and stirred in at the end. Adds a briny, intensely lemony note that transforms the whole sauce.
A teaspoon stirred through for adults — adds heat and a roasted pepper complexity. Also excellent kept at the table.

sauces.name: Groundnut Stew
sauces.sw_note: 2-3 tbsp peanut butter split 5 ways — roughly 1-2 syns per portion

recipe_5.method: Soften aromatics, toast spices 1 min. Add tomatoes and peanut butter — stir well to combine before putting in the oven. 180°C oven 25-30 mins. Thickens naturally from the peanut butter.

elevate.tip: One whole pepper in the stew for the last 15 minutes, removed before serving — infuses flavour without the full hit of heat.
A teaspoon of dried ground crayfish (from African food shops) adds the authentic umami note that defines a real groundnut stew.

recipe_5.method: Soften onion, garlic, ginger. Add spices, toast 1 min. Add tomatoes and paste. 180°C oven 25-30 mins. Stir in lime juice and coriander at the end.

elevate.tip: Replace half the paprika with this for a deep red colour and a mild, complex heat that's very different from regular chilli.
A teaspoon of dried fenugreek, rubbed between your palms and stirred in at the end. The secret finishing touch in every restaurant-quality curry.

sauces.name: Coconut & Lime
sauces.sw_note: Light coconut milk ~2.5 syns per 100ml — one tin (400ml) across 5 portions
sauces.adult_heat_note: Chili oil or fresh chili at the table

recipe_5.method: Soften aromatics with lemongrass paste. Add coconut milk and fish sauce. Simmer gently 15-20 mins — don't boil hard or the coconut milk splits. Add protein with enough time to cook through. Stir in lime juice and coriander at the very end. Fish sauce is strong — taste before adding more.

elevate.tip: 2–3 torn leaves added with the coconut milk, removed before serving. Adds the aromatic citrus note that defines Thai cooking.
Use instead of (or alongside) regular coriander at the very end — aniseed-forward and quite different. Very authentic.

sauces.name: Lemongrass Broth
sauces.adult_heat_note: Fresh chilli or chilli oil at the table

recipe_5.method: Gently soften onion and garlic. Add lemongrass paste and cook 1 min. Add stock and fish sauce — taste before adding more, it's very salty. Simmer 15 mins below a boil. Add lime juice and coriander off the heat. Lighter than Thai with no coconut milk — clean, fragrant and very good with fish and prawns.

elevate.tip: One or two simmered in the stock and removed before serving — adds the aromatic backbone of a proper pho.
A teaspoon alongside the lime juice adds another layer of acidity and a slightly different brightness.

sauces.name: Five Spice Wok
sauces.sw_note: Miso is synned — check brand. Soy sauce is free.

recipe_5.method: High heat throughout. Stir-fry aromatics until just softening. Add five spice, toss 30 secs. Add stock, soy, miso, vinegar. Cook protein and veg in the sauce. Thicken with granules at the end.

elevate.tip: A splash into the hot wok before the stock — adds the characteristic flavour that separates restaurant Chinese cooking from home versions.
A tablespoon stirred in adds glossy, savoury depth. Worth keeping in the fridge — it lasts months and transforms stir-fries.

recipe_5.method: Gently warm stock with garlic and ginger — keep it below a boil. Whisk miso in off the heat or on very low (boiling degrades it). Add soy and vinegar. Taste as you go — it's delicate. Thicken lightly with granules. Garnish with spring onion.

elevate.tip: A teaspoon adds a subtle, clean sweetness that rounds out the saltiness of the miso and soy — don't use more or it tips too sweet.
Replace the stock cube with instant dashi for a more authentic Japanese flavour base. Huge difference for very little effort.

sauces.name: Soy & Miso
sauces.sw_note: Miso synned. Gochujang for adults is low-syn — check brand.
sauces.adult_heat_note: Gochujang paste on the side — also doubles as a table chili sauce for Mexican and Chinese

ingredients: few drops sesame oil to finish (synned — a little goes a long way)
recipe_5.method: Soften aromatics. Add stock, soy, miso, vinegar. Simmer 10-15 mins. Thicken with granules. Finish with just a few drops of sesame oil — it's very strong, don't overdo it. Adults add gochujang at the table.

elevate.tip: A tablespoon for adults — the fermented chilli paste that defines Korean cooking. Stir in at the end or keep at the table.
A teaspoon adds subtle sweetness and gloss. The combination of miso, soy and mirin is the foundation of Korean and Japanese sauces.

recipe_5.method: Mix and press into meat. Simple and clean — lets the protein do the work. Good on fish fillets in the oven or chicken with roasted potatoes.

elevate.tip: A few sprigs of fresh instead of dried — the difference in aroma is significant. Worth keeping a small pot on the windowsill.
A teaspoon mixed in acts as a binder and adds a gentle sharpness that works particularly well with chicken and fish.

ingredients: 1 tsp dried basil (or use fresh, chopped, after cooking)
recipe_5.method: Mix and press into the meat. Leave 15 mins if you have time, cook straight away if not. Air fryer at 190°C for 20-25 mins for chicken thighs. Works brilliantly tossed through pasta with roasted veg — no sauce needed.

elevate.tip: A pinch, lightly crushed and added to the rub — particularly good with pork and sausage. Very Italian.
A small smear rubbed into the meat under the herbs before they go on. Disappears completely but adds remarkable depth.

rubs.name: Adobo
rubs.adult_heat_note: Chili flakes mixed into adults' portion after cooking

recipe_5.method: Mix and coat. Air fryer or griddle pan. Good on chicken thighs sliced and served in wraps or over rice with lime and coriander.

elevate.tip: Replace or supplement the smoked paprika for a deeper, more complex smokiness with subtle heat.
The juice and zest of half an orange in the mix adds brightness and sweetness — particularly good with chicken.

rubs.name: Jerk
rubs.adult_heat_note: This is already the mild version — adults can add hot sauce

recipe_5.method: Mix into a paste. Coat chicken thoroughly — score the meat if thighs so it gets in. Ideally marinate 1hr+. Air fryer at 190°C for 25 mins or oven at 200°C. The allspice is the key flavour — don't substitute.

elevate.tip: Blend one into the marinade for adults — this is the defining heat of proper jerk and really cannot be substituted.
A tablespoon in the wet marinade. Make sure the marinating time is long enough for the alcohol to work into the meat.

recipe_5.method: Mix into a rough paste with the lemon juice. Coat the meat. Oven or air fryer. The lemon juice helps it stick and caramelises nicely. Serve with couscous and scatter fresh coriander or parsley over.

elevate.tip: Finely grated rind mixed into the rub instead of (or alongside) fresh lemon juice — more concentrated and aromatic.
A teaspoon in the rub or scattered over after cooking — adds a herbaceous, sesame note that bridges North African and Middle Eastern.

ingredients: thumb of ginger, grated (or 0.5 tsp ground)
recipe_5.method: Mix into a paste with the lemon juice. More complex than any single-cuisine rub — go gently until you know it. Particularly good on lamb shoulder or chicken thighs. Oven or air fryer at 190°C. The allspice is what makes it Ethiopian rather than North African.

elevate.tip: A tiny pinch, lightly toasted and ground — adds a slightly bitter, maple-like note that's a classic berbere ingredient.
A teaspoon in the paste helps caramelisation and tempers the spice complexity — particularly good on chicken.

ingredients: thumb of ginger, grated (or 0.5 tsp ground ginger)
recipe_5.method: Mix into a paste with lime juice. Coat chicken and leave at least 20 mins — an hour in the fridge is better. Air fryer or oven at 200°C. The turmeric will colour the meat golden.

elevate.tip: Replace all the paprika with this for the deep red-orange colour and gentle, complex heat of an authentic tandoori.
Half a teaspoon rubbed between your palms and mixed in — dried fenugreek is the ingredient that makes tandoori taste like tandoori.

recipe_5.method: Mix and coat. Marinate at least 20 mins — longer is better. The soy acts as a brine as well as a flavouring. Air fryer, griddle, or oven. Good on salmon fillets or chicken thighs over rice.

elevate.tip: A teaspoon in the marinade adds gloss and subtle sweetness that helps caramelisation — the key to a proper teriyaki finish.
A few drops only — extremely strong, but adds the nutty finish that characterises Japanese and Korean cooking.

recipe_5.method: Mix into a paste. Score pork or chicken deeply and work the marinade in — at least 1 hour, overnight is better. The five spice and soy should form a red-brown glaze after cooking. Air fryer or oven at 200°C, basting with leftover marinade halfway through.

elevate.tip: A tablespoon in the marinade adds the glossy sweetness that defines restaurant char siu — a small jar lasts months.
A teaspoon adds gentle acidity that balances the soy and helps the glaze caramelise evenly.

dressings.name: Balsamic + Dijon
dressings.sw_note: Balsamic ~1 syn per tbsp. Keep to 1 tbsp across the whole salad.

recipe_5.method: Whisk together. The Dijon emulsifies it so it coats leaves evenly without oil. Slightly richer than a plain vinegar dressing — good on warm salads or with roasted veg.

elevate.tip: A few drops of the proper thick, syrupy kind instead of regular balsamic — completely different product. A little goes a very long way.
A very finely minced small shallot stirred in — the standard addition to a correct French dressing and worth doing every time.

dressings.name: Dijon Vinaigrette
dressings.notes: Proper vinaigrette without the oil — the Dijon holds it together.

recipe_5.method: Whisk vinegar into Dijon. Add shallot. Toss through leaves just before serving — not before or they'll wilt.

elevate.tip: A very finely minced small shallot is the thing that separates a real French vinaigrette from everything else. This is the correct way to make it.
A few leaves, finely chopped — the defining herb of French salads, particularly good with anything involving chicken.

dressings.name: Caper Lemon
dressings.notes: Barely qualifies as a dressing — more of a seasoning. No oil needed.

recipe_5.method: Squeeze lemon over, scatter capers, crack pepper. That's it. Add a little caper brine from the jar if you want extra punch.

elevate.tip: One fillet mashed to a paste — invisible in the dressing but adds a savouriness that makes everything taste more of itself.
A few fronds work beautifully with capers and lemon. Particularly good over poached salmon or a warm potato salad.

ingredients: handful flat-leaf parsley or fresh coriander, chopped
recipe_5.method: Mix and drizzle. Light and fresh — works anywhere you want brightness without weight.

elevate.tip: A very finely minced small shallot, left to macerate in the lemon juice for 10 minutes — mellows the rawness and adds real depth.
A teaspoon of finely chopped rind instead of (or alongside) fresh lemon — more complex, more aromatic, and very different.

recipe_5.method: Mix and toss through. Good as a slaw dressing or over a Mexican-style chicken salad. Bright and clean.

elevate.tip: Half a jalapeño, very finely minced and stirred through — adds heat without overpowering. Particularly good in a Mexican slaw.
Half a teaspoon to balance the acidity of the lime. Synned, but a small amount makes a noticeable difference — taste as you go.

dressings.name: Tahini Lemon
dressings.sw_note: ~3 syns per tbsp tahini — 1 tbsp across 5 portions is about 0.6 syns each

recipe_5.method: Whisk tahini and lemon together — it'll seize up first, keep going. Add water gradually until it's a pourable consistency. Drizzle over roasted veg or falafel.

elevate.tip: Scattered over the top after drizzling — adds herby, sesame crunch that's particularly good over roasted vegetables or falafel.
A teaspoon drizzled alongside — the sweet-sour contrast with tahini is a classic Middle Eastern combination.

dressings.name: Nam Jim
dressings.notes: A Thai dipping sauce that doubles as a punchy dressing. Fish sauce is very strong — add gradually.

recipe_5.method: Mix and taste — it should be salty, sour and very fragrant. Fish sauce is the dominant flavour so build slowly. Use as a dressing, dipping sauce or light marinade. Keeps in the fridge for a few days.

elevate.tip: Half a bird's eye finely sliced — the proper version has chilli heat. Keep at the table for adults.
Half a teaspoon dissolved in the lime juice is the classic balance to the fish sauce saltiness.

dressings.name: Ginger Lime
dressings.notes: Add a few drops of sesame oil if you have syns to spend — transforms it.

recipe_5.method: Mix and drizzle. Works cold over noodles, shredded chicken or raw veg. Punchy — a little goes a long way.

elevate.tip: Just a few drops — very strong, but adds the nutty depth that lifts this from a dressing into something restaurant-quality.
Half a teaspoon dissolved in the lime juice — balances the acidity and adds the subtle complexity that defines Thai dressings.

dressings.name: Miso & Ginger
dressings.sw_note: Miso is synned — check brand. Two tablespoons across 5 portions is minimal.

recipe_5.method: Whisk together and thin with water until it pours easily — miso thickens it significantly. Taste for balance: you may want a little more vinegar. Works cold over soba noodles, shredded cabbage, roasted sweet potato or cucumber.

elevate.tip: A few drops transforms this into something restaurant-quality. Extremely strong — less than you think.
A teaspoon instead of some of the water — adds subtle sweetness and makes the dressing glossier.
